Volts · David Roberts 2 episode(s) · 102 insights

Building a big, abundant, clean grid121 min52 insights2026-09-16
▶ Watch on YouTube
Clean-energy policy analyst Jane Flegel tells Volts host David Roberts that US electricity demand growth from the data-center buildout is a once-in-a-generation chance to finance a much larger clean grid, and that the binding constraint is now federal permitting and the total absence of grid planning rather than technology cost. She argues the risks of underbuilding dwarf the risks of overbuilding, warns that behind-the-meter gas could supply more than half of new US data-center capacity by 2028 with roughly 100% gas emissions rates, and pushes for a federal or state fund capitalized by hyperscalers plus a federal permitting deal covering NEPA, the Clean Water Act and interregional transmission siting.
Industrial policy vs. carbon pricing · 4IRA retrospective · 4Green groups and philanthropy critique · 4Data center bargain and grid funds · 6Behind-the-meter gas risk · 6Grid planning and clean firm · 6Utility incentives and affordability · 6Permitting reform math · 10Republican strategy and 2029 agenda · 6
Industrial policy vs. carbon pricing 4
Jane Flegel argues carbon pricing cannot work as the primary climate lever because carbon, unlike HFCs or conventional pollutants, is embedded throughout the entire economy rather than concentrated in a few producers and geographies with ready substitutes.
framework🗣 Jane Flegelconviction: highcarbon pricingMontreal ProtocolHFCsJane Flegel
So what: Investors should discount scenarios where a US carbon price re-emerges as the central decarbonization mechanism and instead underwrite subsidy-, procurement- and permitting-driven policy regimes.
“Carbon unlike these other pollutants is embedded deeply kind of everywhere in the economy.” ▶ 11:35
The 'green spiral' theory Flegel works from holds that government investment drives clean-tech costs down, deployment creates industries and jobs, and those industries then become a political constituency powerful enough to demand more climate policy.
framework🗣 Jane Flegelconviction: highNina Kelseygreen spiralsolarbatterieswind
So what: Policy durability tracks industry scale and lobbying capacity, so sectors with large installed bases and employment footprints are the better bets for surviving hostile administrations.
Flegel cites roughly 90% cost declines for solar and for batteries and about 70% for wind as evidence the cost-decline leg of the green spiral worked, while the political-power leg largely failed.
data_point🗣 Jane Flegelconviction: highsolarbatterieswind
So what: Cheap hardware is no longer the differentiator; political and permitting execution is where returns now diverge across clean-energy assets.
“we have 90% cost declines for solar and batteries and incredible same for batteries, 70% for wind” ▶ 12:26
Flegel says climate advocates cannot defeat entrenched fossil interests with 'a coalition of the marginalized' and must instead recruit part of capital onto their side, the way the New Deal did.
contrarian🗣 Jane Flegelconviction: highfossil fuel industryNew Dealclimate advocacy
So what: Signals that clean-energy trade groups and hyperscalers, not environmental NGOs, are the coalition partners whose lobbying spend will determine future US energy policy.
“you are not going to roll them with like a coalition of the marginalized. It's the same way that the New Deal worked. You got to have some part of capital on your side.” ▶ 13:21

Flegel's first mechanism against behind-the-meter gas is resource-mix dilution: a grid-connected data center draws a blended emissions rate including zero-marginal-cost renewables, nuclear and hydro plus efficient combined cycle, whereas an off-grid facility runs at effectively 100% gas.

Flegel's second mechanism is that off-grid data-center generation is optimized for speed rather than thermal efficiency, producing simple-cycle and aeroderivative turbines running near 100% capacity factor that are arguably worse than coal, plus diesel and kerosene backup.
causal🗣 Jane Flegelconviction: highsimple cycle turbinesaeroderivative turbinescoaldieselkerosenedata centers

Flegel argues permitting reform asymmetrically advantages clean energy because solar and wind require roughly 20 and 200 times respectively the permitted land area of gas per unit of energy delivered, and transmission rights of way run two to three times wider than a comparable gas pipeline.

Flegel cites federal land avoidance as the overlooked NEPA dynamic: federal lands are 21% of the lower 48 but host only 3% of US onshore wind, solar and geothermal capacity, despite the disproportionately federal desert southwest having the country's best solar and geothermal resources.

How to build a more flexible, quieter, less obnoxious data center75 min50 insights2026-09-16
▶ Watch on YouTube
Varys CEO Nelson Abramson, a two-decade Google data center veteran, tells David Roberts how his Sidewalk Infrastructure Partners-backed startup replaces diesel generators with large LFP battery arrays, evaporative cooling towers with air-cooled chillers, and low-voltage distribution with a medium-voltage power plane — claiming up to 77% utilization of provisioned utility capacity versus ~49% conventionally. He also defends the company's noise, water and by-right-industrial-land claims for its stalled Lyon Township (Michigan) and Salem (Oregon) projects, where the Oregon governor pulled a public land sale and recall petitions were launched against council members who approved the Michigan site.

Energy-asset premise and integration case 7
Varys CEO Nelson Abramson argues that at 500 MW to 1 GW campus scale a data center should be underwritten as an energy asset rather than as industrial real estate, which is the framing that opens up power-side design innovation.
framework🗣 Nelson Abramsonconviction: highVarysNelson Abramsondata centers
So what: Investors screening data center developers should test whether a sponsor prices grid interconnection and storage as the core asset, not square footage, since that determines margin per interconnect.
“It's really an energy asset that happens to consume real estate.” ▶ 4:52
Abramson frames data centers as conversion engines from utility capacity into compute capacity, making any gain in compute-per-provisioned-watt a first-order value driver because utilities can only deliver so many watts per location.
framework🗣 Nelson Abramsonconviction: highVarysutilitiescompute capacity
So what: In a grid-constrained buildout, efficiency of the interconnect — not land or shell cost — becomes the scarce input that sets developer returns.
Data center capacity has scaled 50–100x over roughly 30 years — from Abramson's first sub-1 MW site in a converted Hechinger's hardware store to next-generation Nvidia racks at over a megawatt each — while the core electrical and mechanical design template stayed essentially unchanged.
data_point🗣 Nelson Abramsonconviction: highNvidiaHechinger'sdata centers
So what: A design template that scaled by replication rather than redesign is the opening Varys is attacking; incumbents carrying that template may face a cost-per-compute disadvantage.

Capital Allocators · Ted Seides 1 episode(s) · 69 insights

AI in the Investment Office: 8 CIOs on What’s Working127 min69 insights2026-09-16
▶ Watch on YouTube
Ted Seides interviews eight allocator CIOs — spanning a one-person single family office to CPP Investments' $580bn — on exactly how AI is deployed inside investment offices today. The consensus: Anthropic's Claude plus Microsoft Copilot are the default stack, the real bottleneck is proprietary data organization rather than model capability, almost everyone has deliberately stopped short of letting AI make or recommend investment decisions, and only JP Morgan's alternatives team and CPP claim any measurable alpha or decision-quality gain so far.

The Watchdogs of AGI — Rune Kvist of AI Underwriting Company87 min53 insights2026-09-16
▶ Watch on YouTube
Rune Kvist, co-founder of AI Underwriting Company (AIU), announces a $40M Series A led by Ribbit Capital and argues the binding constraint on AI adoption is liability and trust rather than capability, to be solved with a quarterly-updated agent security standard plus insurance capacity from Lloyds of London. He details how certification works for customers like Cursor, Harvey, Lovable, 11 Labs and Sierra, why standards must precede insurance, and why an independent third party will be needed between frontier labs and governments at the model layer because labs can never be their own watchdog.

The Immigration Industrial Complex | Callum Smiles96 min52 insights2026-09-16
▶ Watch on YouTube
A UK-focused interview with researcher Callum, who has filmed in the Calais/Dunkirk migrant camps and the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, laying out the money flows behind Channel crossings: ~£3,000 boat seats with summer discounts to £1,000, NGO-supplied SIM cards, 4,767 National Lottery grants worth £324.8m tied to migration since 2004, and government accommodation contracts such as the MOD's 1996 sale of 57,000 homes to Annington and its £6bn buyback of 36,347 of them in December 2024. The host pairs this with a domestic-decay thesis — national debt at £3 trillion and 94% of GDP versus £527bn and 36% in 2007, London flats down ~20%, visibly emptier West End restaurants — and both conclude the answer is 'parallel institutions', pitching the Wyvern Fellowship at £5/month or £50/year with its first local chapter launching in about two weeks. Despite the channel's Bitcoin branding, there is no bitcoin or crypto discussion in this episode.
Channel crossing unit economics · 7Asylum demand marketing · 3NGO funding pipeline · 5Government contracts as the real trade · 9Gig-economy black market · 2Ceuta border surge · 7UK fiscal and consumer decay · 11Parallel institutions play · 8
Channel crossing unit economics 7
A seat on a small boat across the Channel costs roughly £3,000, with advertised summer discounts as low as £1,000, so a single 200-person crossing grosses around £200,000 for the smuggling network and a 50-person boat at full price grosses £150,000.
data_point🗣 Callum (guest, researcher who films in the Calais camps)conviction: highCalaisChannel crossingspeople-smuggling gangsAlbanian gangs
So what: Puts a revenue number on the smuggling trade: enforcement that does not destroy the per-boat margin (interception after launch, rescue at sea) leaves the business model intact, because the operator has already been paid.
“So a grand each, that's a 200 grand crossing. It's good money.” ▶ 13:27
Smugglers deliberately oversell seats on each boat so that the buyers left behind on the beach stay mixed into the crowd, because French police cannot arrest people merely for wanting to board and therefore cannot distinguish traffickers from migrants.
framework🗣 Callum (guest)conviction: highpeople-smuggling gangsFrench policeCalais
So what: Explains why arrest counts on the French coast stay low regardless of spending: the operating model is designed to defeat identification, so headline enforcement statistics are a poor proxy for disruption.

“they would look at tidal maps and basically if waves were over 5T they wouldn't send any out.” ▶ 18:05

So what: Ties the border question to a domestic organised-crime labour supply: the debt, not the crossing, is what creates the ongoing criminal economy inside the UK.

TWIML AI Podcast · Sam Charrington 1 episode(s) · 48 insights

From Voice Agents to AI Avatars64 min48 insights2026-09-17
▶ Watch on YouTube
Alex Mhola, co-founder and CEO of Bosan AI, argues that real-time voice AI is fundamentally a cost-per-conversation problem rather than a pure intelligence problem, and that his team deliberately optimized for price first — claiming benchmark parity-or-better versus GPT, Gemini and Grok at roughly one-tenth the cost with thinking disabled. He details the token-rate-versus-parameter-count tradeoff that governs voice economics, a ~100 million hour proprietary audio corpus stored in an owned data center, and a two-stage architecture where a conversational front end fires background tool/MCP calls while stalling naturally. He predicts audio becomes 'pretty much bulletproof' in about a year and audiovisual avatars — including animated faces on robots — start appearing in roughly a year to eighteen months, with voice being only an intermediate stepping stone toward them.

Voice latency and interruption physics 6
Bosan AI targets interruption handling within roughly 150 milliseconds because that is approximately the biological latency from a photon hitting the retina to the cortex processing it, making it the natural bar for feeling responsive to a human.
framework🗣 Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)conviction: highBosan AIvoice AIneuroscience
So what: Gives an objective, falsifiable latency spec to benchmark any voice-agent vendor against: sub-150ms barge-in, not just fast first-token time.
“it takes about 150 milliseconds for you know basically a photon hitting your retina to your cortex actually doing something with it” ▶ 6:39
Human audiovisual perception effectively operates at only about 6 to 10 hertz, which caps how much temporal fidelity a real-time conversational model actually needs to deliver regardless of display refresh rates.
data_point🗣 Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)conviction: highhuman perceptionvoice AI
So what: Sets a ceiling on useful spend: vendors paying for fidelity above human perceptual limits are burning compute margin for no user-detectable gain.
“humans kind of operate at around maybe 6 to 10 hertz really when it comes to audio visual perception” ▶ 7:20
Single-microphone capture will never solve multi-speaker noise cancellation for voice agents; microphone arrays are required, which pushes a meaningful share of voice-AI quality onto device hardware and OS-level audio stacks rather than the model.

So what: Voice-agent performance is partly captured by device makers; model vendors without a strong hardware partner face a quality ceiling in real-world noisy deployments.
“having a single microphone will probably never really solve this. You need microphone arrays to really do proper noise cancellation” ▶ 3:50

Token-rate vs parameter-count tradeoff 5
Voice models face a hard dilemma where high audio fidelity requires a high token frequency, and a high token frequency forces the model to have fewer parameters because both prefill and generation costs scale with tokens per second.
framework🗣 Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)conviction: hightokenizationLLM inferencevoice AI
So what: Explains why voice-native models will stay structurally smaller than frontier text models, and why 'just scale it' is not available as a strategy in this segment.
“many tokens per second means your model cannot have too many parameters” ▶ 9:23
Text is the ultimate compressed format at roughly three to five tokens per second for human consumption, while audio easily requires ten-plus tokens per second, so a 10-token-per-second audio stream gives each token about 100 milliseconds of temporal granularity.
data_point🗣 Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)conviction: hightokenizationaudio modelstext models
So what: A concrete multiplier for modeling inference cost of voice versus text products: roughly 2-3x the token throughput per second of conversation.

Invest Like the Best · Patrick O'Shaughnessy 1 episode(s) · 48 insights

Sequoia Legend Michael Moritz: Steve Jobs, Being an Outsider, and Investing in the Age of AI94 min48 insights2026-09-16
▶ Watch on YouTube
Michael Moritz, the former Sequoia leader who backed Yahoo, Google-era Silicon Valley, Stripe and Instacart, talks with Patrick O'Shaughnessy about his new family memoir and, through it, his operating beliefs: judge people by their first 14 years, expect monomania to produce greatness at the cost of relationships, and never assume political or institutional stability. The conversation is mostly biographical and historical rather than a markets discussion, but it contains explicit views that early-stage venture's structural edges (imperfect information, real founder relationships) have been competed away, that AI will create more jobs than it destroys, and that Elon Musk may be the greatest industrialist in American history.
Exit timing and the survivor instinct · 4Political risk in the West · 6Reading founders: the first 14 years · 6Monomania and what it costs · 5Venture capital then versus now · 7Running and preserving Sequoia · 7AI, growth rates, and the great-person theory · 9Compression, voice, and judging communication · 4
Exit timing and the survivor instinct 4
Michael Moritz contrasts his two grandfathers as a case study in exit timing: the paternal one, a Bavarian judge with a state pension and faith in institutional durability, stayed in Germany until it was too late and was deported; the maternal one, a blind cattle trader with no institutional attachment, got out 72 hours before war broke out.
framework🗣 Michael Moritzconviction: highGermanyBavariaNazi Germany
So what: A reusable model for regime-change and drawdown risk: the asset that keeps you in a deteriorating position (a pension, a franchise, a sunk career) is what makes you late; people with portable, self-generated income exit early.
“they got out um 72 hours before war broke out. So 72 hours later, they too would have perished.” ▶ 11:04
Moritz argues the barriers to exiting a deteriorating regime are underestimated — leaving 1930s Germany required finding a country that would accept you and paying large exit taxes to the Nazi government, so the option to leave decays even for those who decide to.
causal🗣 Michael Moritzconviction: highNazi Germany
So what: Optionality is perishable: capital controls and access restrictions tighten precisely when you most want to move, which argues for pre-positioning rather than waiting for confirmation.
“You had to find a place elsewhere that would accept you. You had to pay big um um taxes to uh the Nazi government in order to be able to secure your exit visas.” ▶ 9:26
Moritz's personal operating rule drawn from his family history is to always maintain a fallback jurisdiction, which he summarizes as never being able to hold too many passports — and he says this feels especially relevant in the present environment.
thesis🗣 Michael Moritzconviction: highUnited StatesWestern Europe
So what: A prominent long-horizon allocator is explicitly thinking about personal and jurisdictional diversification, a signal that domicile and residency planning is live among wealthy families.
“the uh necessity for always feeling that you have a bolt hole, that you have someplace to go if the fire gets too hot” ▶ 13:37
Moritz says the drive he attributes to his own success came not from stories his refugee parents told — they never told them — but from absorbed daily behavior: an expectation that doom was near, suspicion of others' motives, and constant vigilance.
causal🗣 Michael Moritzconviction: highMichael Moritz
So what: Suggests that when assessing a founder's resilience, observed household behavior and posture matter more than the narratives a family consciously transmits.
“It was definitely not the stories they told because they didn't tell the stories” ▶ 5:56

Lex Fridman Podcast 1 episode(s) · 48 insights

Psychiatry, Insane Asylums, Mental Illness, ECT, Lobotomies, Freud & Jung | Lex Fridman Podcast #502217 min48 insights2026-09-17
▶ Watch on YouTube
Historian of psychiatry Andrew Scull argues to Lex Fridman that psychiatry is in crisis on three fronts at once: a DSM diagnostic system built for reliability rather than validity that leading NIMH directors themselves denounced, a roughly $20 billion bet on genetics and neuroscience that Thomas Insel conceded improved patients' lot 'not one bit,' and a drug arsenal that is no real advance on the accidental discoveries of the 1950s. He traces a repeating historical pattern in which desperate remedies (Henry Cotton's organ removals, malaria therapy, insulin coma, lobotomy, unmodified ECT) each claimed roughly 80% cure rates, won Nobel Prizes, and died from generational turnover or a rival technology rather than from evidence, and warns that ketamine and psychedelics are being hyped as miracle depression cures on enormously weak evidence.
DSM diagnostic crisis · 6The failed biological bet · 5Desperate remedies playbook · 6Degeneration to T4 · 5ECT's contested evidence · 5Psychoanalysis displaced by CBT · 7Drug economics and efficacy · 8Hype, trust and the research pipeline · 6
DSM diagnostic crisis 6
The DSM-III task force led by Robert Spitzer in 1980 deliberately built psychiatric diagnosis as a symptom-checklist system optimized for reliability (two clinicians reaching the same label) rather than validity (the label matching an underlying reality), and that same architecture still underpins diagnosis today.
framework🗣 Andrew Scullconviction: highDSM-IIIRobert SpitzerColumbiapsychiatry
So what: Every downstream commercial structure built on DSM categories - drug indications, insurance reimbursement codes, clinical trial endpoints - rests on a classification its own architects only claimed was consistent, not true.
“That didn't mean necessarily it was a valid diagnostic system” ▶ 10:21
DSM-5 was launched in the early 2000s with the explicit goal of rebasing diagnosis on underlying pathology using the decoded human genome and neurotransmission research, but by about 2008 its authors gave up and fell back on the 1980 symptom-based approach.
data_point🗣 Andrew Scullconviction: highDSM-5human genomePCRneurotransmission
So what: A decade of genomics and neuroscience investment failed to produce a single biologically grounded psychiatric diagnosis, a cautionary base rate for anyone underwriting precision-psychiatry claims.
When DSM-5 was published, Thomas Insel and Steven Hyman - the then-current and preceding directors of the National Institute of Mental Health - publicly denounced it as unscientific and useless, while DSM-III's Robert Spitzer and DSM-IV's Allen Frances attacked it for being produced in secrecy.
data_point🗣 Andrew Scullconviction: highThomas InselSteven HymanNIMHDSM-5Robert SpitzerAllen Frances
So what: The field's own institutional leadership has disowned the manual that still governs reimbursement and regulatory approval, a legitimacy gap that eventually forces revision of what counts as a treatable indication.
“denounced the document as unscientific and useless” ▶ 25:05
Psychiatric genetics has undermined rather than confirmed the DSM categories: roughly three hundred small genome variations account for only about ten percent of schizophrenia, and the genetic abnormalities raising susceptibility to bipolar disorder, schizophrenia and autism overlap heavily.
data_point🗣 Andrew Scullconviction: highgenome-wide association studiesschizophreniabipolar disorderautism
So what: If the diagnostic boxes are not genetically distinct entities, drug development targeting them by label is aiming at constructs rather than diseases, which helps explain repeated late-stage CNS trial failures.
“if we use three hundred small variations in the genome, we can account for about ten percent of schizophrenia” ▶ 1:35:41
Some leading psychiatrists are speculating that within ten years the field will have to concede there is no such thing as schizophrenia or bipolar disorder as discrete illnesses, and Scull expects that admission to further damage public trust in psychiatry even though it is where the science points.
prediction🗣 Andrew Scullconviction: mediumschizophreniabipolar disorderRobin Murraypsychiatry
So what: A category collapse of this scale would reset clinical trial design, diagnostic coding and the entire marketing architecture of psychiatric drugs within a decade.
“there's no such thing as schizophrenia, there's no such thing as bipolar disorder” ▶ 1:36:50
Scull describes 'diagnostic creep' as a recurring mechanism in which a core of unambiguous severe cases expands into a surrounding penumbra, and cites DSM-IV chief editor Allen Frances's conviction that the huge rise in autism diagnoses came more from Frances loosening the criteria than from more actual cases.
causal🗣 Andrew Scullconviction: highAllen FrancesautismDSM-IVNick HaslamNAMI
So what: Diagnosed prevalence growth in psychiatric conditions can be a criteria artifact rather than a real epidemiological trend, which inflates addressable-market estimates built on diagnosis counts.
“the huge increase in the number of diagnoses of autism is more driven by the fact he loosened the criteria for the diagnosis” ▶ 3:17:13
The failed biological bet 5
Thomas Insel, after running NIMH for about thirteen years and funding an enormous volume of genetics and neuroscience research, conceded that roughly $20 billion of spending left the lot of the mentally ill improved not one bit.
data_point🗣 Andrew Scullconviction: highThomas InselNIMHneurosciencegenetics
So what: The single largest public research bet in mental health produced no measurable patient benefit, the clearest available prior on expected returns from brain-disease-first approaches to mental illness.
“after spending 20 billion dollars, the lot of the mentally ill has improved not one bit right?” ▶ 13:14
Scull characterizes the field's half-century swing with Leon Eisenberg's line that psychiatry moved from brainless to mindless, meaning the enthusiasm for neuroscience discarded psychological and social insight just as the Freudians had earlier discarded biology.
framework🗣 Andrew Scullconviction: highLeon EisenbergHarvardneurosciencepsychoanalysis
So what: A field that oscillates between total explanatory models rather than integrating them will keep producing decade-long research fashions that end in disappointment.
“When I entered psychiatry, it was brainless psychiatry, leaving it mindless psychiatry.” ▶ 17:46
Everything psychiatry currently offers is symptomatic treatment rather than cure, with no equivalent of penicillin for any psychiatric condition, and treatments themselves generate iatrogenic harm - Scull cites PTSD exposure therapy making a significant share of patients worse.
thesis🗣 Andrew Scullconviction: highPTSDantipsychoticsantidepressantspsychotherapy
So what: Framing psychiatric products as symptom management with a real harm tail, rather than as cures, is the honest base case for both clinical expectations and liability exposure.
“We don't have a psychiatric penicillin for any of the conditions we're gonna be talking about” ▶ 4:10
Neuroscience failed to throw up new drug targets, so pharmaceutical companies concluded they could make more money researching other diseases and abandoned mental illness, leaving a drug set that Steven Hyman says is no real advance on the compounds found by accident in the 1950s.
causal🗣 Andrew Scullconviction: highSteven HymanBig Pharmaneurosciencepsychiatric drugs
So what: Major pharma has structurally exited psychiatric drug discovery, leaving new development to small startups - which concentrates both the opportunity and the risk in early-stage CNS biotech.
Despite cataloguing psychiatry's biological failures, Scull says he would be astonished if the major forms of mental illness did not have a biological component, and calls the absence of research by the players with the most money to develop better treatments depressing.
thesis🗣 Andrew Scullconviction: highBig Pharmamental illnessdrug development
So what: The critic's own position is that the biological pipeline is underfunded rather than misguided, which argues the pharma retreat is a capital-allocation failure rather than a verdict on the science.
“the fact that there's no research being done by the people with the most money to develop better treatments is well, one word for it would be depressing” ▶ 3:31:04
Desperate remedies playbook 6
Scull identifies a recurring 80 percent cure claim as the signature of therapeutic overreach in psychiatry, appearing in the early asylums, in Henry Cotton's surgical work and in insulin coma therapy alike, and explicitly maps that pattern onto present-day breakthrough rhetoric.
framework🗣 Andrew Scullconviction: highHenry Cottoninsulin coma therapyasylums
So what: A reusable screening heuristic: implausibly round, high cure rates in a field with no biomarker are a historical marker of claims that will not survive controlled trials.
“80% cure for Cotton's work, 80% cure for insulin coma therapy, 80% cure for the early asylums. This is overblown rhetoric” ▶ 1:38:43
Henry Cotton, head of the New Jersey State Mental Hospital at Trenton from 1916, treated madness as focal sepsis and progressively pulled teeth, removed tonsils, stomachs, spleens and colons while claiming to cure eighty percent of patients, even though 45 percent of those given abdominal surgery died within a year.
data_point🗣 Andrew Scullconviction: highHenry CottonTrenton State Hospitalfocal sepsisAdolf Meyer
So what: An institution can sustain a treatment with a near-50 percent one-year mortality for decades when outcome measurement is controlled by the practitioner.
“Stomachs are like cement mixers on a construction site and could be dispensed with.” ▶ 1:11:51
Cotton's work was validated by the highest-status gatekeepers of its day - a prestigious Princeton lecture series, publication by Oxford and Princeton University Presses, and a New York Times write-up hailing it as a great breakthrough - and his successors continued pulling teeth and tonsils until 1960.
causal🗣 Andrew Scullconviction: highPrinceton University PressOxford University PressThe New York TimesHenry Cotton
So what: Elite institutional endorsement is not an independent check on therapeutic claims; it can be the mechanism that entrenches them for forty years.
Two of psychiatry's only Nobel Prizes went to interventions later discredited: Wagner-Jauregg's 1937 award for infecting general paralysis of the insane patients with malaria, and Egas Moniz's 1949 medicine prize for lobotomy, awarded just fourteen years after the procedure was invented.
data_point🗣 Andrew Scullconviction: highWagner-JaureggEgas MonizNobel Prizelobotomygeneral paralysis of the insane
So what: The field's top external validation signal has a documented false-positive rate on exactly the kind of dramatic intervention it is asked to adjudicate.
“Moniz wins the Nobel Prize in medicine in 1949 for lobotomy” ▶ 52:20
Insulin coma therapy for schizophrenia, claimed by Sakel to cure eighty percent of patients, required a course of up to sixty comas, carried a one to five percent mortality rate and caused brain damage and obesity, and survived from 1933 until a randomized controlled trial in the 1950s failed it.
data_point🗣 Andrew Scullconviction: highSakelinsulin coma therapyschizophreniaJohn NashHarlem Valley Mental Hospital
So what: The controlled trial, not accumulating clinical experience, was the only thing that terminated a two-decade treatment - the decisive argument for demanding trial evidence before scale-up.
“It turned out to have a mortality rate of one to five percent” ▶ 1:19:25
Lobotomy ended not through evidence but through generational turnover plus the arrival of a rival technology, as younger psychiatrists who saw the incontinent back-ward casualties rebelled and had antipsychotic drugs available that looked more like regular medicine.
causal🗣 Andrew Scullconviction: highWalter Freemanlobotomyantipsychotics
So what: Discredited practices in medicine are displaced by substitutes and cohort replacement rather than refuted by data, which sets the realistic timeline for any entrenched standard of care being unseated.
“I could teach any damn fool to perform a lobotomy in twenty minutes even a psychiatrist.” ▶ 54:20
Degeneration to T4 5
Asylums founded on the promise of curing 60 to 80 percent of patients were actually discharging only 35 to 40 percent, so each year left behind a residue of chronic patients until the accumulated chronic population came to define the institution's public image.
causal🗣 Andrew Scullconviction: highasylumsalienists
So what: A stock-versus-flow accounting error - measuring cures against annual admissions while chronic cases accumulate - can make a genuinely partially effective institution look like a total failure.
“They were discharging 35 or 40% of their patients” ▶ 38:39
When asylum cure rates were exposed as nearer 10 to 12 percent, the profession blamed the patients by adopting degeneration theory - casting them as evolutionary throwbacks with defective brains - which converted the asylum from a therapeutic project into a custodial one.
causal🗣 Andrew Scullconviction: highdegeneration theoryasylumseugenics
So what: When a professional promise fails publicly, redefining the population as untreatable is a cheaper institutional response than admitting the method failed, and it licenses far worse policy.
California pioneered forced sterilization of mental patients and continued the practice until about 1960, with over 60,000 sterilizations performed in the US by the 1960s and California accounting for a disproportionate share.
data_point🗣 Lex Fridmanconviction: highCaliforniasterilizationeugenics
So what: Coercive population policy ran inside a modern democratic state for roughly four decades, a reminder of how long institutional practice can outlive the discredited theory that justified it.
“over 60,000 sterilizations have been performed in the US” ▶ 41:24
The Rockefeller Foundation chose psychiatry as its priority investment area around 1930, partly because several trustees had mental illness in their own families, and among the geneticists it funded was Ernst Rudin in Germany, who became a leading proponent of sterilization and then of murdering mental patients.
causal🗣 Andrew Scullconviction: highThe Rockefeller FoundationErnst RudinGermanygenetics
So what: Concentrated private philanthropy in a field with weak science can export an ideology as effectively as it funds research, a governance risk wherever one funder dominates a nascent discipline.
The mentally ill were the first victims of the Final Solution through Hitler's T4 program, which killed as many as a quarter million people and was where the gas chamber and the technique of disguising it as showers were developed, and German psychiatry for the most part collaborated.
data_point🗣 Andrew Scullconviction: highT4 programTiergartenstrasse 4Nazi GermanyGerman psychiatry
So what: The professional class closest to the patients supplied the rationale and the personnel, which is why Scull treats internal professional dissent as an insufficient safeguard compared with external checks and balances.
“which may have been as many as a quarter million people, that the technology of the gas chamber was developed” ▶ 43:25
ECT's contested evidence 5
In mental hospitals through the 1940s, 50s and 60s, ECT was overwhelmingly deployed as a punitive instrument of behavioral discipline and control rather than as a therapeutic intervention, with patients moderating their own behavior to avoid repeat treatments.
contrarian🗣 Andrew Scullconviction: highECTmental hospitals
So what: The historical case against ECT is really a case against institutional incentives, which is why modern evidence about the procedure and public sentiment about it have diverged so sharply.
“ECT was much more used as a device to control people's behavior, than as a therapeutic intervention” ▶ 1:26:23
Introducing muscle relaxants and anesthesia eliminated the spinal and hip fractures of unmodified ECT but made it a more complicated procedure requiring anesthesiologists and breathing support, while memory loss remains a widely recognized and disputed price of treatment.
data_point🗣 Andrew Scullconviction: highECTcurareanesthesiology
So what: The modification that made ECT safe also made it capital and staff intensive, which constrains supply independently of clinical demand.
Scull concedes that recent controlled trials provide decent evidence that ECT works for some severely distressed and suicidal depression patients, while stressing that it is a purely empirical treatment with no understood mechanism and typically requires repeat maintenance sessions rather than curing anything.
thesis🗣 Andrew Scullconviction: mediumECTtreatment-resistant depressionsuicidal depression
So what: A treatment can be evidence-backed and mechanistically opaque at the same time; the opacity, not the evidence, is what keeps adoption and reimbursement suppressed.
The film of One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest fixed public opposition to ECT for decades and still creates hesitation today, and in California ECT now almost cannot be given to involuntarily confined patients because consent is required - an unusual legal constraint for a medical procedure.
causal🗣 Andrew Scullconviction: highOne Flew Over the Cuckoo's NestKen KeseyJack NicholsonCaliforniaECT
So what: A single cultural artifact produced durable regulatory and utilization effects on a medical technology, the clearest case in the conversation of narrative risk outweighing clinical data.
Treatment-resistant depression is defined purely by failure to respond to drugs rather than by any distinct underlying disease, which Scull flags as a conceptually revealing label.
framework🗣 Andrew Scullconviction: hightreatment-resistant depressionantidepressants
So what: An entire commercial category is defined by the failure of the incumbent product class rather than by biology, so its size is a function of how poorly existing drugs work.
Psychoanalysis displaced by CBT 7
Psychoanalysis originated with Breuer's patient Anna O. (Bertha von Pappenheim) and the notion that repressed memories resurface as physical and psychological symptoms, and Freud replaced hypnosis with free association only after concluding he was a clumsy hypnotist and learning that Charcot's hypnotized hysterics in Paris had been performing rehearsed routines.

So what: The founding evidence base of the twentieth century's dominant therapeutic paradigm was a handful of case vignettes built on a technique its originator had already found to be partly theatrical.
Freud's 1909 Clark University lectures, retrospectively framed as a Freud conference, were actually an afterthought at a thirty-speaker event that included two Nobel physics laureates and Franz Boas, and mainstream American psychiatry dismissed talk therapy for what it regarded as a biological condition.
data_point🗣 Andrew Scullconviction: highSigmund FreudClark UniversityFranz BoasWilliam JamesJames Jackson Putnam
So what: In-house histories systematically inflate the founding moment of a paradigm, so origin stories told by a field about itself deserve the same discount as management's account of its own track record.
Freud himself lamented that his case histories read like short stories and therefore lacked the stamp of serious science, which Scull argues is precisely why novelists, playwrights, screenwriters and surrealists embraced psychoanalysis while clinical psychiatry did not.
causal🗣 Andrew Scullconviction: highSigmund Freudpsychoanalysissurrealism
So what: Cultural adoption and scientific validation are separate distribution channels, and a theory can dominate the first for fifty years while failing the second.
“my case histories read like short stories” ▶ 2:28:39
Jung, not Freud, captured the wealthiest American patrons - a McCormick heir to the International Harvester fortune, Edith Rockefeller McCormick who wrote him big checks, and Paul and Mary Mellon whose foundation subsidized Princeton University Press publishing his works - and Scull suggests that patronage gap probably exacerbated the 1913 Freud-Jung split.
anecdote🗣 Andrew Scullconviction: mediumCarl JungSigmund FreudMcCormick familyEdith RockefellerPaul MellonPrinceton University Press
So what: Patron capital shaped which branch of psychoanalysis got published and institutionalized, an early example of funding determining which intellectual franchise survives.
Psychoanalysis could never scale: circa 1930 roughly three hundred analysts in North America each seeing patients five hours a week could treat only a few thousand people while hundreds of thousands sat in mental hospitals, and its training institutes sat outside the universities just as universities were becoming the post-war knowledge factories.

Rockefeller Foundation funders Alan Gregg and Robert Morison repeatedly pressed analysts for proof their treatment worked and were refused on the grounds that reconstructing entire personalities cannot be measured, while clinical psychologists built training that included two years of scientific research methods and consequently knew how to win federal grants that the analysts could not obtain.

Drug economics and efficacy 8
Chlorpromazine, the compound that launched modern psychopharmacology, was an 1880s antihistamine that Rhone-Poulenc handed out to see if it might work as an antiemetic, an eczema treatment or an anesthetic potentiator, and only became a psychiatric drug because naval surgeon Henri Laborit noticed his pre-surgical patients stopped caring and wrote that it worked like a chemical lobotomy.
anecdote🗣 Andrew Scullconviction: highchlorpromazineRhone-PoulencHenri LaboritDelay and DenikerSaint-Anne's
So what: The foundational asset of an entire drug class was found by unplanned repurposing in an era with no trial controls, not by targeted discovery.
“this works like a chemical lobotomy” ▶ 2:55:56
The first two American drug companies approached to license chlorpromazine declined on the view there was no market, but SmithKline & French bought it and within two years two million people were taking the drug, transforming the firm from a small operator into a big company.
data_point🗣 Andrew Scullconviction: highSmithKline & FrenchchlorpromazineThorazineLargactil
So what: The largest psychiatric franchise of the century was twice passed over by incumbents who misjudged the market, and the buyer's advantage came from sales execution rather than science.
“within two years, two million people are taking this drug” ▶ 2:58:18
SmithKline & French created demand by putting its best salesmen on state legislatures and politicians with moving pictures of agitated patients turning calm, precisely because hospital psychiatrists were not yet interested in the idea of a chemical treatment.
causal🗣 Andrew Scullconviction: highSmithKline & Frenchstate legislaturesBig Pharma
So what: Where the clinical customer is unconvinced, the budget holder can be sold instead - the original template for pharmaceutical policy marketing that still shapes psychiatric drug adoption.
Major tranquilizers were renamed antipsychotics in the early 1960s, implying they attacked the underlying psychosis, but they only dampen the positive symptoms of hallucination and delusion for a subset of patients and do little or nothing for the negative symptoms of apathy, language poverty and lost social capacity.

The 2005 NIMH-funded CATIE study published in the New England Journal of Medicine found that the newer patented second-generation antipsychotics, up to ten times more expensive than the off-patent first-generation drug, were not more efficacious, and that between 67 and 82 percent of patients dropped out of the trial depending on the drug.

“Between 67% and 82% of the patients, depending on which drug they were on, dropped out of the trial” ▶ 3:09:47
Second-generation antipsychotics traded one iatrogenic harm for another, reducing tardive dyskinesia somewhat while causing weight gain of 10 to 50 pounds that brings metabolic syndrome, diabetes and heart trouble.
data_point🗣 Andrew Scullconviction: hightardive dyskinesiametabolic syndromediabetessecond generation antipsychotics
So what: Side-effect substitution rather than elimination means the long-run cost burden of the newer drugs shifts to cardiometabolic care rather than disappearing.
SSRIs beat placebo by a statistically significant but not clinically significant margin - improvement of one or two points on a 60-point rating scale can clear statistical significance - while over forty percent of depressed patients do not respond at all, many suffer emotional numbing and loss of libido that sometimes never returns, and withdrawal can be severe enough to trap patients on the drugs.
data_point🗣 Andrew Scullconviction: highSSRIsProzacZoloftPaxilserotoninLancet
So what: The most prescribed antidepressant class delivers modest average benefit with a large non-responder tail and a dependency dynamic, which is the central vulnerability for both litigation and displacement by alternatives.
“for most patients, antidepressants are marginally better than placebo, but a lot of the effect is the placebo effect” ▶ 3:23:15
FDA approval required only two positive trials regardless of how many failed, so a sponsor could run fifteen trials with thirteen failures and still win approval, while drug companies funded the studies, owned the data and released only what helped them.

So what: The approval standard itself institutionalizes publication bias, so the apparent efficacy of any approved psychiatric drug is an upper bound rather than an estimate.
“You might have conducted 15 trials and 13 of them had been failures, but if you had two that worked, that was enough.” ▶ 3:08:37
Hype, trust and the research pipeline 6
Scull says ketamine and psychedelics are currently being propounded as a miracle cure for depression on evidence that is enormously weak, and explicitly places this in the same pattern as the repeated 80 percent cure claims of the asylum, insulin coma and focal sepsis eras.

Scull locates the hype problem not only in science journalism but inside the gatekeeping journals, arguing Science and Nature foreground findings that make a big splash while negative findings, which are what prevent mistakes, do not get published.

So what: The selection filter for breakthrough claims runs through the journals themselves, so discounting hype requires discounting the primary literature and not just its press coverage.

So what: The damage compounds on a multi-year lag and shows up as an absence of future discoveries rather than as a visible event, so the cost will not appear in any near-term data series.
“it takes at least six or seven years to train a scientist at the beginning of their career” ▶ 1:33:21
Scull treats institutional trust as an asset that is slow to build and fast to destroy, warning that vaccination distrust is generalizing into broad distrust of science and medicine and that mistrust will grow exponentially over four years.

Annie Lowrey on the Time Tax, Fraud, and Rationing by Paperwork58 min47 insights2026-09-16
▶ Watch on YouTube
Atlantic staff writer Annie Lowrey argues with Tyler Cowen that US government programs ration benefits by paperwork rather than by price or rules, costing roughly 50 hours per person per year, with the burden falling hardest on poor people, immigrants and people entangled with the criminal justice system. Cowen repeatedly presses the contrarian case that administrative friction is a useful rationing and screening device — for Medicare procedures, disability, immigration and even voting — while Lowrey counters that fraud is overwhelmingly provider-side, that improper payments are a function of rule complexity, and that simpler federal administration plus AI agents would cut both burden and fraud. She also concedes her earlier pro-UBI book was too optimistic about ancillary benefits, while arguing AI-driven white-collar disruption revives the UBI case.

The Great Simplification · Nate Hagens 1 episode(s) · 43 insights

The Opportunities of a World in Collapse with Sarah Wilson | TGS 23498 min43 insights2026-09-16

Author Sarah Wilson, on Nate Hagens' podcast, argues the 'meta-crisis' is a simultaneous convergence of nuclear, AI, climate, food/water, financial and trade-route crises that no government, market or technology can fix, and that the correct posture is abandoning 'hopium' for truth, community bonds and radical simplification. The concrete hooks are European energy and civil-preparedness stress (French forward gas near $25/MMBtu vs $3 in the US, EU-wide 72-hour survival-kit advisories, Macron converting hospitals for wartime readiness), a sharply revised peak-population timeline of 2040–2060 at barely 10 billion with Taiwan/South Korea fertility at 0.7–0.8, and their shared view that the single largest near-term risk in wealthy countries is mass civil unrest, not physical climate impacts.

What Francis Fukuyama Is Seeing at ‘The End of History’ | Odd Lots56 min37 insights2026-09-17

Francis Fukuyama tells Odd Lots hosts Tracy Alloway and Joe Weisenthal that the discontent driving global illiberalism is not material but 'thymotic' — a demand for recognition that markets, UBI and AI-driven abundance cannot satisfy — and that dignity derived from paid work is the thing AI is most likely to destroy. He argues China is the only plausible non-liberal competitor but that Xi Jinping's double-down on high-tech export-led growth is destroying other countries' manufacturing bases and stoking backlash, while liberal societies have accumulated so much procedural rule of law that they can no longer build visible things.

A Brookings analyst of the US and Europe walks through the AfD's near-44% showing in the September 6 Saxony-Anhalt state election, arguing the party is materially more radical than Le Pen's or Meloni's parties, is anti-EU, anti-euro and functionally anti-NATO with a stated preference for close ties to Russia and China, and that a German party ban is legally available but politically self-defeating. The stakes are framed as European rather than German: with two more state elections on September 20, a wobbling Merz coalition, Le Pen polling well for 2027 and daily Russian shadow-warfare incidents against European infrastructure, the guest argues the stability of Europe now turns on whether German centrist parties can deliver credible governance.

Forward Guidance · Blockworks 1 episode(s) · 31 insights

The Market Is Mispricing A Correlation Shock | Dean Curnutt54 min31 insights2026-09-16
▶ Watch on YouTube
Dean Curnutt, CEO of Macro Risk Advisors and host of the Alpha Exchange podcast, argues that realized correlation among S&P constituents has collapsed to 5-15% — levels with no historical comparison — which is artificially suppressing index volatility and the VIX, making S&P and VIX optionality cheap relative to a stack of live risks. He contends AI/hyperscaler names that currently trade as uncorrelated will prove highly correlated after the fact, and that with the 10-year note behaving as the risk asset rather than the hedge, investors should own S&P vol, VIX calls and VIX call spreads systematically rather than trying to time the event.

Record-low S&P stock correlation 6
Realized correlation among S&P constituent stocks has been running roughly 5-15% for about a year and a half, a level with no comparison in the last five, ten or twenty years of data.
data_point🗣 Dean Curnuttconviction: highS&PMacro Risk Advisors
So what: The entire cheapness of index volatility rests on a correlation regime that has no historical precedent, so any mean reversion mechanically reprices index vol higher.
“you can only go back one month or three months or a year” ▶ 6:21
Historical benchmarks for stock correlation are roughly 35-40% in benign markets and 75-90% in crises such as LTCM, the GFC and the 2011 sovereign debt/US debt ceiling episode, versus 5-15% today.
data_point🗣 Dean Curnuttconviction: highLTCMGFCS&Psovereign debt crisis
So what: Provides the calibration for how far correlation could travel in a shock — a move from 10% toward 75%+ is a multi-fold repricing of index vol, not a marginal one.
Even during 2026's shock episodes realized correlation only reached about 35%, meaning the peak in recent stress equals what used to be the benign-market average — evidence something structural has changed.
data_point🗣 Dean Curnuttconviction: highS&P

Jason’s Put a $5K Bounty on His Dream Chrome Extension | E233840 min28 insights2026-09-16
▶ Watch on YouTube
The hosts of This Week in Startups review round one of a $5,000 public bounty to build annotated.com, a Chrome sidebar extension for highlighting and commenting on articles, X posts and video clips, scoring three vibe-coded submissions 8.5, 8 and 6 out of 10 and judging all three close to shippable on web. The episode doubles as a case study in AI-driven build-cost collapse — the same product priced at roughly $500,000 twenty years ago now attracts a $5,000 bounty — and lays out three monetization paths for the winner: incubation inside the host's venture firm, an unmonetized Reddit-style social network burning about $250,000 a year, or selling expert annotations as training data to LLM companies. A closing listener segment features a homeless founder with two pre-revenue startups, where both hosts advise securing income and shelter before attempting to raise.

Chat With Traders 1 episode(s) · 26 insights

The Man Who Introduced Candlestick Charting to the West · Steve Nison46 min26 insights2026-09-16
▶ Watch on YouTube
Steve Nison, the technical analyst who brought Japanese candlestick charting to Western markets in the late 1980s, explains how he built an information monopoly by paying to translate 13-14 Japanese charting books, quietly used candles to generate the top-performing recommendation track record at his brokerage, and then seeded global adoption through a Futures magazine article, a Merrill Lynch reference guide that drew 10,000+ requests, and direct lobbying of charting vendors. The practical core of the conversation is his copyrighted 'Trading Triad' — candle signal plus Western technical confirmation plus risk/reward — alongside a hard rule to place a protective stop at the moment of entry and to trade the market's reaction to news rather than a prediction of the news.

Steve Nison discovered candlestick charting around the late 1980s only because a Japanese broker at his firm kept a candlestick chart book on her desk, and she told him Japan had been using the technique since before 1900 — a roughly century-long information asymmetry between Japanese and Western technicians.
anecdote🗣 Steve Nisonconviction: highJapancandlestick chartstechnical analysis
So what: Durable edges can sit in plain sight inside another language or market culture; scanning foreign-language practitioner literature is a repeatable way to source non-consensus method.
“This traditional form of charting candlestick uh candlestick uh analysis we've been using in Japan before 1900.” ▶ 0:13
At the time Nison began his research, Bloomberg was the only charting service in the West that displayed candlestick charts, and it carried them solely to serve its Japanese clients.
data_point🗣 Steve Nisonconviction: highBloombergcandlestick chartsJapan
So what: Vendor coverage is a proxy for how widely a technique is actually used; a method supported by one terminal for one client base is close to untraded information.
“back then the only charting service that had candlesticks was Bloomberg. And the reason for that was because of their Japanese clients.” ▶ 0:22
Nison personally funded the translation of 13 or 14 Japanese candlestick books over roughly a year, using an American trader who spoke Japanese and was already traveling to Japan, and separately cross-checked pages by fax with members of the Nippon Technical Analyst Association reached through his Market Technicians Association membership.
anecdote🗣 Steve Nisonconviction: highMarket Technicians AssociationNippon Technical Analyst AssociationJapancandlestick charts
So what: Shows the concrete cost structure of a research moat — money, a year of after-hours time, and professional-network access — which is exactly what deterred competitors.
Nison's son demonstrated that an AI tool instantly translated a page of the same Japanese source books that had cost Nison a year and substantial money to have translated, and the output matched the human translator's version.
causal🗣 Steve Nisonconviction: highAIJapancandlestick charts
So what: The specific moat Nison monetized — cross-language document access — has collapsed to near-zero cost, implying today's translation-based research edges decay fast and edge must come from interpretation, not access.
“He took a picture of one of the pages. Boom. It was translated and I compared it to what the translator done.” ▶ 10:48
Undisclosed Edge at the Brokerage 2
Once Nison understood candlesticks, he issued trade recommendations to brokers across the firm based primarily on candlestick signals while deliberately not disclosing the method, and per the host he held the firm's highest-performing recommendation track record.
anecdote🗣 Steve Nisonconviction: highcandlestick chartsMerrill LynchEF Hutton
So what: A worked example that edge decays on disclosure — the performance was harvested during the window when the method was private.
“I would make the recommendations basically based on candles, but I didn't tell them that.” ▶ 11:15
Nison argues candlesticks had many timing advantages and no offsetting disadvantage, and that the only real barrier was the time and effort required to decode them — which is likely why nobody in the West had done it before him.
causal🗣 Steve Nisonconviction: highcandlestick chartstechnical analysis
So what: Identifies effort-gated rather than insight-gated opportunities: where the only barrier is grunt work, the edge persists until someone is willing to pay the labor cost.
“There was no disadvantage at all except for the time and effort it took me to do it. And maybe that's why nobody else did it.” ▶ 12:03
Seeding Global Adoption 2
Nison actively lobbied charting software vendors to add candlesticks — writing to companies to tell them CQG had already added them — and timed that push to coincide with his book's release so his book would be the only available source of instruction.
framework🗣 Steve Nisonconviction: highCQGBloombergcandlestick charts
So what: A template for standard-setting: push the tooling into distribution first, then own the only education layer on top of it.
“I started to write to other companies letting them know that hey this company has uh candlestick charts maybe you should think about doing it and that's when my book was coming out.” ▶ 23:54
Nison's book made an explicit prediction that candlestick charting would take over and bar charts would essentially disappear — a call that was validated, since candlesticks are now the default chart type on virtually every trading platform.
prediction🗣 Steve Nisonconviction: highcandlestick chartsbar charts
So what: A resolved forecast on format adoption: a strictly dominant presentation of identical data displaces the incumbent once the education friction is removed.
“there's absolutely no downside to using a candlestick chart maybe a little bit of education” ▶ 24:29
Trading Triad Framework 4
Nison's copyrighted 'Trading Triad' requires three things before a trade: a candlestick signal, confirmation from a Western technical signal, and an acceptable risk/reward — and he says he has never seen anything comparable in the Japanese source material, which does not discuss risk/reward.
framework🗣 Steve Nisonconviction: highTrading Triadcandlestick chartstechnical analysis
So what: A concrete three-filter checklist that converts pattern recognition into an executable process, with the risk leg as the Western addition.
“if I had to break it down to three critical ones, candle signal is a confirming a western signal or vice versa. Is a western signal confirm a candlestick signal and riskreward.” ▶ 34:00
Because candlestick signals are typically used to pick tops and bottoms — inherently high-risk trades — Nison insists on stacking the odds with confirmation from simple Western tools, favoring basic horizontal support and resistance under a 'keep it simple' principle.
framework🗣 Steve Nisonconviction: highcandlestick chartssupport and resistancetechnical analysis
So what: Counter-trend entries need confluence to survive; a signal taken alone at an unconfirmed level is the highest-variance way to use candles.
“you're trying to pick tops and bottoms. Very high risk to begin with. You want the odds in your side.” ▶ 32:51
Nison will pass on even a textbook bullish engulfing pattern with a large green real body if price is only a few ticks below major resistance, preferring to wait for a pullback to the low of the engulfing pattern.
framework🗣 Steve Nisonconviction: highbullish engulfing patternsupport and resistance
So what: Gives a specific veto rule and a defined re-entry level, turning risk/reward from a slogan into a concrete trade filter.
Candlesticks use exactly the same open-high-low-close data as bar charts and therefore work in all markets and all time frames, which is why Nison positions them as a complement to Western techniques like head and shoulders, moving averages and trend lines rather than a replacement.
framework🗣 Steve Nisonconviction: highcandlestick chartsbar chartsmoving averagestrend lines
So what: Zero switching cost and no data requirement beyond OHLC explains both the universal adoption and why candles can be layered onto an existing process without discarding it.
“they work in all markets and all time frames” ▶ 12:42
Stops and Loss Discipline 5
Nison's rule is to enter the protective stop at the same moment the trade is placed and then trail it up as the position moves in his favor, rejecting the common intention to simply exit later if the market goes against you.
framework🗣 Steve Nisonconviction: highrisk managementstop loss
So what: Removes the discretionary exit decision at precisely the moment discretion is most compromised — a directly implementable process change.
“The best time to put in a protective stop is when you do the trade and then if trade goes in your direction, you move up the stop.” ▶ 36:02
Nison says mental stops almost never work because ego makes traders rationalize holding, and in his career he saw only one trader at EF Hutton who could genuinely execute a mental stop without any visible sign of stress.
causal🗣 Steve Nisonconviction: highEF Huttonrisk managementstop loss
So what: Argues the ability to hold a mental stop is rare enough to be treated as an exception, so systems should assume hard stops by default.
According to the host, Nison had more losing recommendations than winning ones yet still produced the highest-performing track record — attributing the result to risk management rather than hit rate.
data_point🗣 hostconviction: mediumrisk managementcandlestick charts
So what: Reinforces that expectancy, not win percentage, drives track records — useful when evaluating strategies or managers on accuracy statistics alone.
Nison's seminar line that the one rule working 100% of the time is 'excellent support at zero' is aimed at traders who scale into a fundamentally cheap position all the way down, and he pairs it with the view that once money is in the market emotion takes over from objectivity.
contrarian🗣 Steve Nisonconviction: highrisk managementfundamental analysis
So what: A blunt warning against averaging down on conviction without a technical stop level — the failure mode that converts a thesis into a permanent loss.
“there's excellent support at zero” ▶ 39:18
Nison frames the entry decision as the last moment of control: when placing a trade the trader is in control, but once in the market the market is in control, which is his justification for pre-committing the stop.
framework🗣 Steve Nisonconviction: highrisk managementtrading psychology
So what: A clean mental model for why all risk parameters should be set pre-trade rather than managed live.
“when you're placing a trade you're in control but once you're in the market the market's in control.” ▶ 39:45
React to News, Don't Predict It 2
Nison argues a trader can be 100% right on a fundamental forecast and 100% wrong on the market reaction, citing recent Middle East conflict and oil where a correct call on crude going to $100 would still have missed markets making record highs.
contrarian🗣 Steve Nisonconviction: highcrude oilMiddle Eastequities
So what: Separates event forecasting from position sizing — being right on macro is not an edge unless the market's response function is also right.
Nison's preferred alternative is to trade the reaction rather than the forecast: a market that refuses to fall on bad news, or that sells off on apparently good news, is giving a directional signal in itself.
framework🗣 Steve Nisonconviction: highprice actiontechnical analysis
So what: A repeatable, low-cost read on positioning and exhaustion around scheduled events, and one that requires no fundamental forecast at all.
“if it's not reacting negatively on bad news that's telling you something and vice versa” ▶ 38:21
Reading Doji, Hammers and Windows 4
Nison treats a doji as a pattern change rather than a reversal signal — it turns a trend from up to neutral, analogous to a car braking rather than going into reverse — which is a common misread among traders who see doji as an automatic top.
framework🗣 Steve Nisonconviction: highdojicandlestick charts
So what: Prevents premature counter-trend entries; a doji is a signal to stop adding, not necessarily a signal to reverse exposure.
Nison says a cluster of small real bodies or doji after a sharp advance can make a market healthier by relieving an overbought condition and letting buyers grow comfortable at the higher level, rather than signalling a top.
contrarian🗣 Steve Nisonconviction: highdojioverboughtcandlestick charts
So what: Reframes post-rally consolidation as constructive base-building, supporting continuation trades where pattern-book reading would call an exit.
Nison uses doji levels as potential resistance areas and treats a close above the doji as a potential breakout trigger.
framework🗣 Steve Nisonconviction: mediumdojisupport and resistance
So what: Converts a single-bar pattern into a defined level with an objective trigger, which is directly testable.
Nison's reading of the Japanese material turns on trend context and closing prices: the same long-lower-shadow shape is a bullish hammer in a downtrend and a bearish hanging man in an uptrend, and the Japanese phrase about price 'momentarily' passing through a window (a gap) means it did not close beyond that level.
framework🗣 Steve Nisonconviction: highhammerhanging manwindowsgapsJapan
So what: Two concrete disambiguation rules — trend context defines the signal, and closes rather than intraday penetration define whether a gap level has failed.
Selling a Method to Skeptical Pros 3
After a first seminar to NYSE specialists pitching candlesticks as superior produced roughly one client, Nison repositioned the identical material as a small timing addition to what the specialists already knew and converted about ten clients from the second session.
anecdote🗣 Steve Nisonconviction: highNYSE specialistscandlestick chartsMarket Technicians Association
So what: Adoption of a new analytical tool by professionals depends on framing it as an add-on rather than a replacement — relevant to anyone selling research or tooling into institutions.
“These people have huge egos and you don't tell them what to do. You make them, they're the experts.” ▶ 27:04
Nison warns that traders picking up isolated pattern definitions from the internet — a hammer, a shooting star, a bullish engulfing — and trading them without knowing what else to incorporate are playing a dangerous game.
thesis🗣 Steve Nisonconviction: highcandlestick chartscandlecharts.comhammer
So what: The commoditization of pattern knowledge has raised, not lowered, the risk for retail traders, since the context rules that made the patterns work did not commoditize with them.
“you'll see it and you may trade or invest in it but without having the correct knowledge what else to incorporate uh is it could be a really dangerous game.” ▶ 43:55
Nison notes the exchange runs both ways: Japanese candlestick books he had translated devote a quarter or more of their content to Western techniques such as moving averages, meaning Japanese traders had been importing Western tools for 50-100 years before the West imported candles.
data_point🗣 Steve Nisonconviction: highJapanmoving averagescandlestick chartstechnical analysis
So what: Undercuts the idea of candlesticks as a pure standalone system and supports the hybrid approach that Nison built his method around.
“they've been using our stuff for, you know, 50 100 years. Now, what do we learn learn from them?” ▶ 35:04

Henrik Zeberg: Why Bonds May Be Too Cheap47 min26 insights2026-09-16

Macro strategist Henrik Zeberg (Swissblock, Zeberg Letter) tells Wealthion's Maggie Lake that the US is late-cycle, not early-cycle: the 12-month average of nonfarm payroll job creation is near a standstill and a 2-3% consumer savings rate means a supply-driven inflation impulse has no one to carry it, making stagflation a narrative rather than a state. He argues Treasuries are mispriced because they are too cheap, equities are set up for a 2000-style blow-off top that could take the Nasdaq to 37,000-39,000 before an Eiffel-Tower crash, and the dollar falls toward DXY 93-94 before a violent bust-driven squeeze higher.

Payroll data hides a labor standstill 3
The 12-month moving average of US nonfarm payroll job creation is running near 50,000 jobs per month, and the latest revision cut the April 2025-to-March 2026 period to roughly 16,000 jobs per month, which Zeberg calls a standstill.

So what: If the smoothed job-creation trend is already at recession-entry levels, growth-sensitive assets are priced off a labor picture the monthly headline is masking.

Zeberg says the 12-month average of US job creation is now lower on a nominal basis than it was going into every recession of the past 50 to 60 years, and worse still when measured as a share of population.
data_point🗣 Henrik Zebergconviction: highUS labor marketrecessionnonfarm payrolls
So what: Gives a falsifiable, chartable monthly test of whether the late-cycle thesis is holding.
“it's lower than it's been going into all recessions 50, 60 years back” ▶ 8:05
The 162,000-job headline print rested on a 44% establishment-survey response rate, the lowest on record, with the missing 56% assumed to have hired like the responders; if the non-responders hired half as fast the number falls toward 120,000 or below, and the BLS's own 90% confidence range spans 40,000 to 280,000 jobs.
causal🗣 Henrik Zebergconviction: highBLSestablishment surveynonfarm payrolls
So what: The imputation and noise band are wider than the market-moving surprise, so fade knee-jerk payroll reactions and wait for revisions.
“It was 44%, which is the lowest we have seen in, you know, as far back we can go.” ▶ 9:05
Inflation needs a consumer to carry it 4
Zeberg's core inflation framework is that a supply shock only becomes sustained inflation if someone can pass it on, so with no demand there is no inflation regardless of oil or commodity spikes.

The 1970s analogy fails because the US consumer savings rate is now 2-3% versus above 10% (and 10-20% at the extremes) in the 1970s, removing the buffer households then used to absorb higher prices and keep an inflationary cycle running.

Underserved category thesis 4
Maitreyi Ramakrishnan argues the collegiate South Asian dance-competition circuit is a 40-year-old real subculture that Hollywood has left entirely unadapted while giving car racing roughly a dozen film franchises, framing it as a mispriced content category.
contrarian🗣 Maitreyi Ramakrishnanconviction: highHollywoodBest of the BestBollywood
